--- title: "Scaling single-cell phenotyping with Cellpose and cloud GPU compute" date: 'January 1, 2025' abstract-title: "Summary" --- ## Summary We present a reusable, cloud-scalable pipeline that pairs Cellpose-SAM segmentation with on-demand GPU compute (Modal and S3) for single-cell phenotyping of high-content microscopy, demonstrated on a two-species yeast panel (*S. cerevisiae* versus *S. pombe*). :::{.callout-note title="AI usage disclosure" collapse="true"} This is a placeholder for the AI usage disclosure. Once all authors sign the AI code form on Airtable, SlackBot will message you an AI disclosure that you should place here. ::: ## Purpose High-content microscopy can generate more images than a single workstation can process in a reasonable amount of time. Segmentation is the computationally intensive step, but arriving at a biological answer often also involves transferring large volumes of image data, provisioning GPUs, running sophisticated segmentation algorithms, and collecting standardized per-cell measurements. In this pub, we present a worked example that handles this entire workflow, pairing Cellpose-SAM [@pachitariu2025cellpose] with on-demand compute to scale segmentation across cloud GPUs. This shortens the path from imaging to biological interpretation and gives readers a pattern they can adapt to their own data rather than assemble from scratch. On a two-species yeast panel, we show: 1. Cellpose-SAM, combined with cloud GPU compute, can efficiently scale single-cell phenotyping across large microscopy datasets. 2. The phenotyping outputs derived from the segmentation resolve gross morphological differences between populations. This pub is aimed at researchers developing high-throughput microscopy workflows or deciding how to scale segmentation and phenotyping. The analysis that follows runs on a dataset of two yeast species (*S. cerevisiae* and *S. pombe*), which is useful for validating the pipeline rather than a source of new biological conclusions. The workflow isn't yeast-specific — the same steps of file I/O, segmentation, parallel execution, and per-cell measurement carry over to other images, though it's best suited to imaging individual cells, such as unicellular organisms or dissociated cell populations, where cells can be segmented cleanly. For background on the tools we build on, see the Cellpose-SAM literature [@pachitariu2025cellpose] and the Modal documentation. ## The pipeline ### How the pieces fit together :::{.callout-note title="Draft figure" collapse="false"} A designed hero figure (in progress with Audrey) will replace the schematic below. The Mermaid diagram is a functional stand-in that captures the intended flow. ::: The workflow is a straight line from raw images to per-cell measurements, with one key property: the segmentation step is identical whether it runs on one machine or hundreds of GPU containers. Scale is a deployment choice, not a code rewrite. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Brightfield ND2s
datasets/<id>/raw/"] --> B["File I/O + preprocessing
arcadia-microscopy-tools"] B --> C["Segmentation
Cellpose-SAM → label masks"] C --> D{"Scale-out
one worker per image"} D --> E["Derived artifacts
masks · overlays · measurements"] E --> F["Analysis
pooled per-cell morphology"] P["Plate map
well → strain"] --> F ``` 1. **Input:** brightfield ND2s in object storage, organized as `datasets//raw/`, with a plate map linking wells to strains. 2. **File I/O and preprocessing:** `arcadia-microscopy-tools` handles ND2 reading, channel and pixel-size metadata, a difference-of-Gaussians bandpass, and percentile rescaling. 3. **Segmentation:** Cellpose-SAM produces label masks; cells at the edge of the field of view are dropped. 4. **Scale-out:** one worker per image is fanned across on-demand GPU containers, each reading from and writing to shared cloud storage. 5. **Outputs (`derived/`):** label-mask TIFFs, outline-overlay JPGs for QC, and per-cell measurement CSVs (regionprops, in microns where the pixel size is known). 6. **Analysis:** pooled per-cell measurements joined to the plate map for morphology comparisons across strains. ### A two-species yeast panel To validate the pipeline, we collected brightfield images of two diploid yeasts chosen for visually distinct morphologies — ovoid budding yeast (*S. cerevisiae* BY4743) and rod-shaped fission yeast (*S. pombe* SP286) — across 16 wells of a 96-well plate. We imaged each well at four fields in a 2×2 grid, yielding 64 ND2 files. The plate map (@tbl-plate-map) links each well to genus, species, strain, and ploidy. Culture, acquisition settings, and software versions are in @sec-methods. At 64 images, the plate is big enough to show cloud GPU scaling in action but small enough to run and inspect end to end. And with eight replicate wells per species, we can work at the well level — comparing per-well medians across the 16 wells rather than treating every cell as an independent measurement (@tbl-features). | Species | Strain | Wells | | --- | --- | --- | | *S. cerevisiae* | `BY4743` | K01–K04, L01–L04 | | *S. pombe* | `SP286` | K05–K08, L05–L08 | : Plate map for the two-species panel {#tbl-plate-map} The metadata from a representative ND2 file (well K01; @tbl-nd2-meta) records the optics and pixel size used across the plate. We use that pixel size to convert the downstream morphology measurements to micrometers. ::: {#tbl-nd2-meta .cell tbl-cap='Acquisition metadata from a representative brightfield ND2 file.' execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to load the example ND2 and extract metadata"} import subprocess from pathlib import Path import pandas as pd from arcadia_microscopy_tools.nikon import parse_nd2 DATASET_ID = "20260611_141152_330" EXAMPLE_ND2 = "WellK01_PointK01_0000_Channelbrightfield_Seq0000.nd2" RAW_DIR = Path("scratch/sample_data") / DATASET_ID / "raw" nd2_path = RAW_DIR / EXAMPLE_ND2 if not nd2_path.exists(): RAW_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) src = f"s3://cloud-scaled-cell-phenotyping/datasets/{DATASET_ID}/raw/{EXAMPLE_ND2}" try: subprocess.run(["aws", "s3", "cp", src, str(nd2_path)], check=True, capture_output=True) except (FileNotFoundError, subprocess.CalledProcessError): from analysis.sample_data import fetch_sample_nd2s nd2_path = fetch_sample_nd2s(DATASET_ID, RAW_DIR, limit=1)[0] meta = parse_nd2(nd2_path) cm = meta.channel_metadata_list[0] pd.DataFrame.from_dict( { "file": nd2_path.name, "channel": cm.channel.name, "objective": cm.optics.objective, "magnification": cm.optics.magnification, "NA": cm.optics.numerical_aperture, "pixel_size_um": cm.resolution.xy_step_um, "exposure_s": cm.acquisition.exposure_time_s, }, orient="index", columns=["value"], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Single-cell segmentation at scale This section covers the main step of the pipeline: segmenting the images and measuring the cells, across the whole plate. Each image is processed the same way regardless of where the computation runs, so we describe that per-image work first and then the two ways of running it. For each of the 64 brightfield fields, the pipeline applies a difference-of-Gaussians bandpass (sigmas 1.6 and 16 px), contrast-stretches the result, and runs Cellpose-SAM [@pachitariu2025cellpose], through `arcadia-microscopy-tools`, to produce a label mask. Cells touching the edge of the field are removed before measurement, since a truncated outline would bias area and shape. The remaining cells are measured with scikit-image regionprops and converted to micrometers using the pixel size recorded in the ND2. The mask is also drawn as a yellow outline over the brightfield, which we use for visual QC. For each image, the pipeline writes three artifacts under the dataset's `derived/` prefix: a label-mask TIFF (`masks/`), an overlay JPG (`overlays/`), and a per-cell measurement CSV (`measurements/`). The same code runs in one of two modes, chosen automatically so the notebook works with or without our cloud infrastructure. Both modes produce the same artifacts, and rerunning the notebook reproduces them. ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Scaled execution (Modal + S3) With our cloud infrastructure, each ND2 is processed by its own GPU worker [@modal]. The worker reads the file from S3, runs Cellpose-SAM, measures the cells, renders the overlay, and writes the three artifacts back to the bucket. Because the files are independent, the plate is processed in parallel. #### Local execution (no cloud account required) Without a cloud account, the same Cellpose-SAM code runs locally, on CPU by default, and writes the same three artifacts to a local `derived/` folder. The ND2 files download from the public Zenodo archive once the record id is set (`CSCP_ZENODO_RECORD_ID` or `ZENODO_RECORD_ID`); until then the local path raises an error naming those variables. On CPU, the plate is processed one image at a time, so it's slower than the GPU version. ::: The plate is run by `run_demo`, which returns the same result object in either mode and prints a summary of how many images finished, how many failed, and the wall-clock time. Two parameters affect the segmentation: we set `diameter=30` (pixels), Cellpose-SAM's usual default cell size, and `cellprob_threshold=3.0`, which is stricter than the library default of 0.0 and is the cutoff we found suppressed debris on these brightfield yeast fields. Both our values and the library defaults are in @tbl-segment-config. ::: {.callout-note title="Choosing a backend and rerunning the segmentation" collapse="true"} Set `CSCP_FORCE_LOCAL=1` to force the local path, or pass `backend="modal"` / `backend="local"` to `run_demo`. Details live in the [setup guide](pages/SETUP.qmd). If you rerun this notebook locally, note that segmenting the full plate on CPU is very slow. Set `LIMIT` to a small number to process only a few images; the rest of the notebook still runs from the pre-computed outputs, so you don't need to segment the whole plate to reproduce the downstream results. ::: ::: {#b282a465 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for processing the full plate"} import time from analysis.runner import run_demo # None processes every ND2. Both backends run the full plate; local CPU is sequential. LIMIT = None BACKEND = "auto" CELL_DIAMETER = 30 # pixels CELLPROB_THRESHOLD = 0.0 started = time.time() run = run_demo( DATASET_ID, limit=LIMIT, backend=BACKEND, diameter=CELL_DIAMETER, cellprob_threshold=CELLPROB_THRESHOLD, ) elapsed = time.time() - started if run.backend == "modal": print(f"[modal] Wrote artifacts to s3://cloud-scaled-cell-phenotyping/{run.output_prefix}/") else: print(f"[local] Wrote artifacts to {run.output_prefix}") print(f"Segmented {len(run.results)} image(s), {len(run.failures)} failure(s) in {elapsed:.1f}s.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Segmenting: 0%| | 0/64 [00:00

``` ::: ::: ### Shape alone separates the two species The per-cell measurements are the pipeline's actual product, so the fair test is whether they support the analysis we would run next. Given nothing but per-cell shape, the two yeasts should separate: *S. cerevisiae* is an ovoid budding yeast and *S. pombe* is a rod. A pipeline that failed this test would not be worth scaling. Two steps follow. First comes the joint distribution of the two features that should carry most of the signal, cell area and eccentricity (@fig-area-ecc). Then every shape feature is ranked by how well it separates the species on its own (@tbl-features). Before those plots, we gate on cell area. Segmentation returns some objects that are not single cells: fragments and debris at the small end, and clumps that Cellpose resolved as a single mask at the large end (the largest object in the full-plate table is about 1,270 μm², 50 times the median *S. cerevisiae* cell). We keep objects between 5 and 100 μm², an area-equivalent circular diameter of 2.5–11.3 μm, which brackets a plausible single yeast cell. The gate is deliberately loose: it drops 1.34% of objects and is not tuned to flatter the analysis. ::: {#7a56e334 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to set up the analysis and gate on cell area"} import arcadia_pycolor as apc import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go from plotly.subplots import make_subplots apc.plotly.setup() GROUP_COL = "species" REFERENCE = "cerevisiae" # the species the others are compared against POSITIVE = "pombe" # the "positive" class for AUC AREA_COL = "area_um2" if "area_um2" in labeled.columns else "area" AREA_LABEL = "cell area (μm²)" if AREA_COL == "area_um2" else "cell area (px)" # Plausible-single-cell gate. 5–100 μm² is an area-equivalent circular diameter of # 2.5–11.3 μm: below it, debris and partial masks; above it, merged clumps. MIN_AREA_UM2 = 5.0 MAX_AREA_UM2 = 100.0 measured = labeled.dropna(subset=[GROUP_COL, AREA_COL]) # The gate is written in μm², so it only applies when the pixel size was known. in_gate = ( measured[AREA_COL].between(MIN_AREA_UM2, MAX_AREA_UM2) if AREA_COL == "area_um2" else pd.Series(True, index=measured.index) ) analysis_df = measured.loc[in_gate].copy() present = list(analysis_df[GROUP_COL].unique()) groups = ([REFERENCE] if REFERENCE in present else []) + sorted( g for g in present if g != REFERENCE ) # Italicized "S. pombe"-style labels and a stable color per species, from the plate map. genus_by_species = plate_map.drop_duplicates(GROUP_COL).set_index(GROUP_COL)["genus"] DISPLAY = {species: f"{genus_by_species[species][0]}. {species}" for species in groups} COLORS = dict( zip(groups, [apc.aegean.hex_code, apc.amber.hex_code, apc.seaweed.hex_code], strict=False) ) n_dropped = int((~in_gate).sum()) print( f"{len(analysis_df):,} of {len(measured):,} cells pass the " f"{MIN_AREA_UM2:g}–{MAX_AREA_UM2:g} μm² gate " f"({n_dropped:,} dropped, {n_dropped / len(measured):.2%})." ) print( f"{len(groups)} species across {analysis_df['well'].nunique()} well(s) and " f"{analysis_df['image'].nunique()} image(s): {', '.join(groups)}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 110,242 of 111,118 cells pass the 5–100 μm² gate (876 dropped, 0.79%). 2 species across 16 well(s) and 64 image(s): cerevisiae, pombe ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-area-ecc .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the area-vs-eccentricity figure"} # Every cell is used for the marginal boxes; the scatter shows a random subsample per # species, since 112,000 overplotted markers read as two solid blobs (and bloat the page). POINTS_PER_SPECIES = 5000 rng = np.random.default_rng(0) def box_stats(values): """Quartiles and Tukey fences for a Plotly box trace built from precomputed statistics.""" q1, median, q3 = np.percentile(values, [25, 50, 75]) iqr = q3 - q1 return dict( q1=[q1], median=[median], q3=[q3], lowerfence=[max(values.min(), q1 - 1.5 * iqr)], upperfence=[min(values.max(), q3 + 1.5 * iqr)], mean=[values.mean()], ) fig = make_subplots( rows=2, cols=2, column_widths=[0.85, 0.15], row_heights=[0.15, 0.85], shared_xaxes=True, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.02, vertical_spacing=0.02, ) for species in groups: cells = analysis_df[analysis_df[GROUP_COL] == species] color = COLORS[species] shown = cells.iloc[ rng.choice(len(cells), size=min(POINTS_PER_SPECIES, len(cells)), replace=False) ] fig.add_trace( go.Scattergl( x=shown[AREA_COL], y=shown["eccentricity"], mode="markers", showlegend=False, marker=dict(color=color, size=3, opacity=0.4, line=dict(width=0)), hovertemplate=f"{species}

ecc. %{{y:.2f}}", ), row=2, col=1, ) # A legend-only proxy, so the key shows a full-size, full-opacity marker. fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers", name=f"{DISPLAY[species]} (n = {len(cells):,})", marker=dict(color=color, size=9), ), row=2, col=1, ) box_kwargs = dict( showlegend=False, fillcolor=color, line=dict(color=apc.charcoal.hex_code, width=1), width=0.45, hoverinfo="skip", ) fig.add_trace( go.Box(**box_stats(cells[AREA_COL].to_numpy()), y=[species], orientation="h", **box_kwargs), row=1, col=1, ) fig.add_trace( go.Box(**box_stats(cells["eccentricity"].to_numpy()), x=[species], **box_kwargs), row=2, col=2, ) fig.update_xaxes(title_text=AREA_LABEL, range=[0, MAX_AREA_UM2], row=2, col=1) fig.update_yaxes(title_text="eccentricity", range=[0, 1.02], row=2, col=1) for row, col in ((1, 1), (2, 2)): # the marginals borrow their scale from the scatter fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, ticks="", showline=False, row=row, col=col) fig.update_yaxes(showticklabels=False, ticks="", showline=False, row=row, col=col) fig.update_layout( width=720, height=560, title="Area and eccentricity split the panel into two populations", legend=dict( x=0.99, y=0.03, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.75)" ), ) apc.plotly.style_plot(fig, monospaced_axes="xy", row=2, col=1) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-area-ecc .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Joint distribution of cell area and eccentricity, with marginal box plots. Scatter points are a random subsample of 5,000 cells per species; boxes use every cell that passed the area gate. ::: ::: The two clouds in @fig-area-ecc barely touch. *S. pombe* traces a tight arc, which is what fission yeast morphology predicts: it grows by extending its tips at roughly constant width, so a cell gets larger and more elongated at the same time, and area and eccentricity rise together over the cell cycle. *S. cerevisiae* instead fills a broad, rounder cloud with a tail toward small area and low eccentricity: mostly small buds. The marginal boxes show where the separation actually comes from. The area distributions overlap substantially, since a large budding yeast is the size of a small fission yeast, while the eccentricity distributions hardly overlap at all. ### Ranking every shape feature Area and eccentricity are two of the nine shape features the pipeline reports. To rank all of them, we use the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for each feature on its own: the probability that a randomly chosen *S. pombe* cell scores higher than a randomly chosen *S. cerevisiae* cell. An AUC of 0.5 means the feature is useless and 1.0 means the two distributions do not overlap at all. It is a rank statistic, so the long tails in these distributions do not distort it. @tbl-features also reports a two-sided Mann–Whitney *$p$*-value on the well-level medians, not on the individual cells. The null hypothesis is that the well-median distributions of a given feature are the same in the two species. Cells from the same well share a field of view, a focus plane, and an illumination profile, so a test across all 113,454 cells (111,929 after the gate) would treat those shared conditions as independent observations and return *$p$* ≈ 0 for every feature. The table instead compares 16 well medians, eight per species. With eight versus eight, the smallest two-sided *$p$*-value is 1.6 × 10⁻⁴, and several features reach it because their well medians do not overlap. Those wells are technical replicates, so the test measures consistency across wells rather than a difference between the species. ::: {#tbl-features .cell tbl-cap='Shape features ranked by how well each one separates the two species (AUC on cells; two-sided Mann–Whitney test on well medians).' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to rank shape features by how well each one separates the species"} from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score # Shape only. Orientation is an arbitrary lab-frame angle, the centroids are positions, and # the brightfield intensities describe illumination as much as they describe the cell. FEATURES = { "area_um2": "area (μm²)", "area_convex_um2": "convex area (μm²)", "perimeter_um": "perimeter (μm)", "axis_major_length_um": "major axis (μm)", "axis_minor_length_um": "minor axis (μm)", "eccentricity": "eccentricity", "solidity": "solidity", "circularity": "circularity", "volume_um3": "volume (μm³)", } FEATURES = {col: label for col, label in FEATURES.items() if col in analysis_df.columns} is_positive = (analysis_df[GROUP_COL] == POSITIVE).to_numpy() well_medians = analysis_df.groupby(["well", GROUP_COL])[list(FEATURES)].median().reset_index() rows = [] for col, label in FEATURES.items(): auc = roc_auc_score(is_positive, analysis_df[col]) _, p_well = mannwhitneyu( well_medians.loc[well_medians[GROUP_COL] == POSITIVE, col], well_medians.loc[well_medians[GROUP_COL] == REFERENCE, col], alternative="two-sided", ) rows.append( { "feature": label, f"median, {REFERENCE}": round(analysis_df.loc[~is_positive, col].median(), 2), f"median, {POSITIVE}": round(analysis_df.loc[is_positive, col].median(), 2), # Flip AUCs below 0.5 so every feature is scored in its discriminating direction. "AUC": round(max(auc, 1 - auc), 3), "well-level p (two-sided)": f"{p_well:.1e}", } ) feature_stats = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("AUC", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True) feature_stats ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Circularity leads at an AUC of 0.993, with eccentricity (0.990) and major-axis length (0.978) close behind — all three are measuring elongation. The size features land lower (convex area 0.937, area 0.933, volume 0.864). The one feature that is barely better than a coin flip is minor-axis length (0.572): fission yeast and budding yeast are about the same width, so a feature that only knew cell width would have almost nothing to work with. ## Discussion and conclusion Pairing Cellpose-SAM with on-demand cloud GPU compute provides a robust way to do high-throughput single-cell segmentation and morphology-based phenotyping. On the two-species yeast panel, the pipeline segmented all 64 fields without a failure, and the per-cell shape measurements separated the two species. Because the segmentation step is the same whether it runs on one machine or across hundreds of GPU containers, scaling mostly means running the same code on more workers, rather than re Nothing here is specific to yeast. The pipeline can be applied to datasets of essentially any size and to essentially any unicellular organism. Since Cellpose-SAM is a generalist model, we'd expect the same workflow to handle other microbes, protists, and cultured cells without retraining. The most immediate extension is fluorescence. The same masks can read per-cell intensity from other channels like reporters, markers, and stains, which turns a shape-only readout into a multi-channel phenotyping assay. We do this routinely in-house, but left it out here only to keep the demo focused on the segmentation-and-scaling pattern rather than any one biological readout. The masks are also a good starting point for richer phenotyping, whether that's CellProfiler-style texture and intensity features or embeddings from pretrained vision models, both of which run on the images and masks the pipeline already produces. A few limits are worth keeping in mind. We judge segmentation by visual QC and by the internal consistency of the derived measurements rather than against a ground-truth labeling. The scaled path relies on paid GPU compute and cloud storage (though the local CPU path runs the same plate sequentially without an account). And it's one dataset with technical, not biological, replicates. That's enough to show the pipeline gives stable, species-resolved phenotypes, but not enough to say anything about the yeast themselves. Taken together, the demo shows a segmentation-and-phenotyping pattern that resolves real morphological differences, runs quickly and inexpensively at screen scale, and should carry from this yeast panel to other organisms and richer phenotypes. ## Methods {#sec-methods} The sections below record how the validation plate was prepared and imaged, and which software versions produced the notebook outputs. ### Sample preparation **Strains and culture.** We imaged two wild-type budding and fission yeast strains: *S. cerevisiae* BY4743 and *S. pombe* SP286, respectively. Strains were streaked from stocks onto agarose plates. *S. cerevisiae* was grown in YPD + 2% dextrose and *S. pombe* in YES + 2% dextrose, and both were incubated for 2 days at 30 °C. For each strain, two colonies (biological replicates) were picked and grown as 5 mL overnight liquid cultures in a 24-well plate, with glass beads in each well to keep cells in suspension. Each biological replicate was paired with a technical replicate, giving four wells per species (eight imaging wells total). Cells were transferred to a glass-bottom, 384-well plate (Cellvis, Product #P384-1.5H-N) for imaging. ### Image acquisition We acquired the images on a Nikon system with NIS-Elements JOBS. Each of the 16 wells was imaged at four fields in a 2 × 2 grid, yielding 64 brightfield ND2 files. Wells within a species are technical replicates. A representative file (@tbl-nd2-meta) was acquired with a Plan Apo λD 40× objective (NA 0.95), a pixel size of 0.1625 μm, and a 0.01 s exposure. Those settings are consistent across the plate, and we use the pixel size to convert spatial measurements from pixels to micrometers. ### Software We ran the published notebook on Python 3.12. Segmentation uses Cellpose-SAM via cellpose 4.2.1.1 and `arcadia-microscopy-tools` 0.5.0. Downstream analysis uses scikit-image 0.26.0 [@vanderwalt2014scikit], SciPy 1.18.0 [@virtanen2020scipy], scikit-learn 1.9.1 [@pedregosa2011scikit], and Plotly 6.9.0 [@plotly]. Modal workers run the same stack in a Debian slim image (`python_version="3.12"`) under modal 1.5.3. Versions are pinned in `uv.lock`. ## Appendix {#sec-appendix} `SegmentConfig` knobs forwarded to Cellpose-SAM, plus the Modal scale-out parameters (@tbl-segment-config). Library defaults match a typical brightfield yeast field. We set `cellprob_threshold` to `3.0` so masks are more conservative on these images; `diameter=30` matches the library default of `None` (30 px). Change them in `run_demo(...)` if your cells differ. We cap `max_containers` at 10 as a courtesy on a shared 100-GPU organizational limit; @tbl-benchmark reports runs above that cap. | Parameter | Library default | Value used | Role | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `diameter` | `None` (30 px) | `30` | Expected cell diameter in pixels | | `flow_threshold` | `0.4` | `0.4` | Mask quality filter (higher is stricter) | | `cellprob_threshold` | `0.0` | `3.0` | Cell-probability cutoff (higher yields fewer, more confident masks) | | `percentile_low` / `percentile_high` | `1.0` / `99.0` | `1.0` / `99.0` | Contrast-stretch window after the DoG bandpass | | `dog_sigma_low` / `dog_sigma_high` | `1.6` / `16.0` | `1.6` / `16.0` | Difference-of-Gaussians sigmas (pixels) before segmentation; `None` skips the filter | | `gpu` | `L4` | `L4` | Modal GPU type | | `max_containers` | `10` | `10` | Ceiling on concurrent GPU workers | : Segmentation and scale-out parameters {#tbl-segment-config}
